To fix (1)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 2 imprecise p values out of 76 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p ≤ .007 The NRF advantage in d′ and accuracy held (all p ≤ .007), as did the Condition and Accuracy effects on confidence (all p < .01) and the Accuracy effect on RT (all p < .001).
p < .01 The NRF advantage in d′ and accuracy held (all p ≤ .007), as did the Condition and Accuracy effects on confidence (all p < .01) and the Accuracy effect on RT (all p < .001).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 1 potential power analysis.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/qwen3.5:4b’ to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: software

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
posthoc paired t-test 32 0.05 0.8 0.51 Cohen’s d NA

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as ‘post-hoc’. Calculating observed power is almost never useful. If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

text
No a priori power analysis was conducted, as this study was designed as an initial validation of a novel paradigm and no directly comparable prior data were available to inform expected effect sizes. Sample size (N = 32) was informed by comparable metacognition stud…

Cells longer than 300 characters are cut (…).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 28 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

To check Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 11 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 0 of 227 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 227 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (11 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents sID, trial, condition while the data has sid, condition, trial. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code).

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 30 distinct packages/libraries: base, broom, coda, dplyr, emmeans, ez, ggeffects, gghalves, ggmcmc, ggplot2, ggpubr, ggsignif, glmmTMB, HDInterval, lattice, lme4, lmerTest, magrittr, metaSDT, patchwork, psych, purrr, pwr, readxl, reshape2, rjags, stringr, tibble, tidyr, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

The repository holds MATLAB code. State the version of MATLAB used in the README, and list any add-ons the code needs (for Stata, the user-written commands installed with ssc install; for MATLAB, the toolboxes), so that readers can run the code with the same software.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 538 files: 73 data, 72 code, 4 documentation, 389 materials.
  • We found 36 tabular data files and extracted 227 columns from 29 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 1 study group (ex1), plus 1 collection-level file (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 7 R workspace files (.RData/.rda) contain no reusable tabular data — only fitted models or saved session objects. Such files need R (and the exact packages used) to open and are not machine-readable. Share the underlying data as CSV (or a documented .sav/.dta) with a codebook so it can be reused without R: fam_conf_ctrl.RData, metad_corr_fit.RData, mratio_mle_results.RData, output_cal.RData, output_nrf.RData, pair_repetition.RData, subjects.RData. We ran automated data-quality checks on 227 columns; 14 columns have at least one potential issue (10 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 3 columns with leading/trailing whitespace; 1 column with numeric values stored as text). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender. 1 of 7 spreadsheet files has at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 227 columns across 29 data files.

Spreadsheet Formatting

We examined 7 spreadsheet files in the repository; 1 has at least one formatting issue.

File Sheet Issue Detail
F4H_Collection_n377_food pictures_nutrient_info_vdec18.xlsx Legend_info Empty rows 9 fully empty rows inside the data range.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 29 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

To check Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed 5 R code files for reproducibility and ran 2 of them (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 2 of 3 scripts ran without error when executed (2 more are run by another script with source()).
  • Of the others, 1 could not run because a package or program was not available.
  • 28 installable dependencies detected.
  • 548 statistics stored from the extracted output; 38 of 68 reported tests matched (55.9%).

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 3 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script.

2 of 3 scripts ran to the end: 1 could not run because a package or program was not available.

Script Result What happened
trials2counts.R Ran inside another script Another script runs it with source(), so it ran as part of that script.
fit_metad_group.R Ran inside another script Another script runs it with source(), so it ran as part of that script.
Calculate_Mratio.R Could not run on our server It needs the R package metaSDT, which we could not install. This is not an error in the script.
Analysis_main.R Ran to the end
Plot_figures.R Ran to the end

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A package could not be installed.

  • Calculate_Mratio.R needs metaSDT.

metaSDT is not on CRAN, and your code does not say where it comes from. If it comes from GitHub or Bioconductor, install it at the top of the script, or name the command in the README, for example remotes::install_github(“user/metaSDT”) or BiocManager::install(“metaSDT”), with the version you used.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 68 statistical tests reported in the paper, 38 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 5 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 trials2counts.R — numeric
2 fit_metad_group.R — none
3 Calculate_Mratio.R trials2counts.R, fit_metad_group.R dependency
4 Analysis_main.R Calculate_Mratio.R dependency
5 Plot_figures.R Analysis_main.R dependency

File paths

1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: MetaBites_triallevel_master.xlsx to ../Data/MetaBites_triallevel_master.xlsx (in Calculate_Mratio.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.

Files not run on their own

2 files only define functions, so running them on their own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

File Used by
fit_metad_group.R Calculate_Mratio.R
trials2counts.R Calculate_Mratio.R

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 5 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 2 were run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
trials2counts.R run_by_source 0.0
fit_metad_group.R run_by_source 0.0
Calculate_Mratio.R dependency_unavailable dependency_unavailable 2.5
Analysis_main.R ran_ok 80.1
Plot_figures.R ran_ok 20.5

Dependency-unavailable errors

1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

File
Calculate_Mratio.R

Calls that install packages in the code

1 call to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like was replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Run by another script

2 scripts are run by another script with source(), so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script’s outcome.

> recency_windows <- c("All Trials"     = "mean_all",

> n_boot <- 2000
> cor_by_window <- function(df) {
>   grid <- expand.grid(Window = names(recency_windows),
>                       Condition = c("Calories", "NRF"),
>                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
>   grid$r <- mapply(function(w, cond) {
>     d <- df[df$Condition == cond, ]

>   }, grid$Window, grid$Condition)
>   grid
> }
> boot_p <- function(boot_stat, obs) {

> }
> r_observed <- cor_by_window(recency_merged)
> by_participant <- split(recency_merged, recency_merged$sID)
> boot_samples <- map_dfr(seq_len(n_boot), function(b) {
>   ids <- sample(names(by_participant), replace = TRUE)
>   cor_by_window(bind_rows(by_participant[ids])) %>% mutate(boot = b)
> }) %>%
>   rename(r_boot = r) %>%
>   left_join(rename(r_observed, r_obs = r), by = c("Window", "Condition")) %>%
>   mutate(Window = factor(Window, levels = names(recency_windows)))
> boot_pvals <- boot_samples %>%

> burnin_thresholds <- c(10, 20, 30)
> burnin_results <- purrr::map_dfr(burnin_thresholds, function(n_burnin) {
>   
>   # Trim first n_burnin trials per subject × condition
>   trials_trim <- trials %>%
>     mutate(Condition = recode(as.character(condition), 
>                               "1" = "Calories", "2" = "NRF")) %>%
>     group_by(sID, Condition) %>%
>     arrange(trial, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
>     slice(-(1:n_burnin)) %>%
>     ungroup()
>   
>   # --- Accuracy and d' ---
>   sdt_stats_trim <- trials_trim %>%
>     group_by(sID, Condition) %>%
>     summarise(hits = sum(correct == 1),
>               n_trials = n(),
>               fas = sum(correct == 0),
>               .groups = "drop") %>%
>     mutate(hit_rate = pmin(pmax(hits / n_trials, 1/(2*n_trials)),
>                            1 - 1/(2*n_trials)),
>            fa_rate  = pmin(pmax(fas / n_trials, 1/(2*n_trials)),
>                            1 - 1/(2*n_trials)),
>            dprime   = qnorm(hit_rate) - qnorm(fa_rate),
>            accuracy = hits / n_trials * 100)
>   
>   dprime_wide <- sdt_stats_trim %>%
>     select(sID, Condition, dprime) %>%
>     pivot_wider(names_from = Condition, values_from = dprime)
>   acc_wide <- sdt_stats_trim %>%
>     select(sID, Condition, accuracy) %>%
>     pivot_wider(names_from = Condition, values_from = accuracy)
>   
>   t_dprime <- t.test(dprime_wide$Calories, dprime_wide$NRF, paired = TRUE)
>   t_acc    <- t.test(acc_wide$Calories,    acc_wide$NRF,    paired = TRUE)
>   
>   # --- Confidence 2x2 ANOVA ---
>   conf_trim <- trials_trim %>%
>     mutate(Accuracy = ifelse(correct == 1, "Correct", "Incorrect")) %>%
>     group_by(sID, Condition, Accuracy) %>%
>     summarise(Confidence = mean(confidence, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
>     mutate(sID = factor(sID), Condition = factor(Condition),
>            Accuracy = factor(Accuracy))
>   anova_conf <- ezANOVA(data = conf_trim, dv = Confidence, wid = sID,
>                         within = .(Condition, Accuracy),
>                         detailed = TRUE, type = 3)
>   
>   # --- RT 2x2 ANOVA ---
>   rt_trim <- trials_trim %>%
>     mutate(Accuracy = ifelse(correct == 1, "Correct", "Incorrect")) %>%
>     group_by(sID, Condition, Accuracy) %>%
>     summarise(RT = mean(RT, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
>     mutate(sID = factor(sID), Condition = factor(Condition),
>            Accuracy = factor(Accuracy))
>   anova_rt <- ezANOVA(data = rt_trim, dv = RT, wid = sID,
>                       within = .(Condition, Accuracy),
>                       detailed = TRUE, type = 3)
>   
>   # --- Assemble results ---
>   cal_acc_mean <- mean(acc_wide$Calories, na.rm = TRUE)
>   nrf_acc_mean <- mean(acc_wide$NRF, na.rm = TRUE)
>   
>   tibble(
>     n_burnin      = n_burnin,
>     cal_acc       = cal_acc_mean,
>     nrf_acc       = nrf_acc_mean,
>     dprime_p      = t_dprime$p.value,
>     acc_p         = t_acc$p.value,
>     conf_cond_p   = anova_conf$ANOVA$p[anova_conf$ANOVA$Effect == "Condition"],
>     conf_acc_p    = anova_conf$ANOVA$p[anova_conf$ANOVA$Effect == "Accuracy"],
>     rt_acc_p      = anova_rt$ANOVA$p[anova_rt$ANOVA$Effect == "Accuracy"]
>   )
> })

Reported vs. reproduced

68 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 38 matched (38 fully, 0 partially) — 55.9% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

MATLAB code, no reproducible output

65 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. Consider depositing the results as well, so they are visible without MATLAB installed: run diary('output.txt') (or diary on) before the analysis and diary off after to save a plain-text transcript of everything printed to the Command Window, or use publish('script.m', 'pdf') (or the Live Editor’s Export/Save As) to generate a single readable document with the code, its output, and any figures together.
