3.3 Asymmetric confidence updating across conditions

Examining the task-level global confidence ratings pre-and post-task, we found a significant main effect of Time (F(1, 31) = 10.30, p = .003, η²G = .036), indicating that global confidence ratings decreased from pre-task (M = 69.3, SD = 16.9) to post-task (M = 63.1, SD = 16.2). There was no significant difference between conditions (F(1, 31) = 0.23, p = .638, η²G = .001). However, we did observe a significant Time × Condition interaction (F(1, 31) = 10.05, p = .003, η²G = .026). In the calories condition, task-level global confidence remained relatively stable from pre-task (M = 67.3, SD = 15.9) to post-task (M = 66.3, SD = 13.6; t(31) = -0.45, p = .657). In contrast, task-level global confidence in the NRF condition significantly decreased from pre-task (M = 71.4, SD = 17.9) to post-task (M = 59.8, SD = 18.1; t(31) = -4.03, Holm-corrected p < .001, dz = -0.71; Figure 4A).

On the block level, global and local confidence were significantly positively correlated in both the calories condition (r(158) = .58, p < .001, 95% CI [0.46, 0.67]) and the NRF condition (r(158) = .58, p < .001, 95% CI [0.46, 0.67]) indicating that participants' block-level global confidence judgements closely tracked their average trial-level confidence within each block, as shown in Figure 4B.

Correlations between block-level global confidence and block segment confidence were explored separately for each condition (calories: r = .42 and .39 for the first and last 5 trials, respectively; NRF: r = .47 and .46). Bootstrap comparisons revealed no significant between-condition differences in any window (all Holm-corrected p = 1.00), indicating statistically equivalent relationships between block-wise local and global confidence across conditions. Mean local confidence across the full block was the strongest independent predictor of block-level global confidence (β = .54, SE = 0.117, p < .001), suggesting that participants integrated information across the entire block when forming block-level global confidence judgements. A small but significant recency effect was also observed, with mean confidence from the last 5 trials independently predicting block-level global confidence (β = .13, SE = 0.053, p = .019). By contrast, mean confidence from the first 5 trials did not contribute independently (β = .07, SE = 0.057, p = .225), providing no evidence for a primacy effect. Adding window × Condition interactions did not improve model fit (χ²(3) = 2.96, p = .398), indicating that Condition did not moderate these effects. Bootstrap pairwise comparisons between windows within each condition showed that, in the calories condition, block-level global confidence was more strongly related to mean confidence across the full block than to either the first five (Holm-corrected p = .030) or last five trials (p = .021).

In the NRF condition, the same pattern did not survive correction (both corrected p = .13), and first-versus last-five comparisons did not differ in either condition (corrected p = 1.00). Supplementary Figure S4 visualises these recency and primacy effects, along with bootstrap comparisons. These results reveal a distinct confidence updating pattern across conditions: participants negatively updated their task-level global confidence for nutritional quality but not for calories, despite showing similar alignment between trial-level and block-level confidence in both domains. updating from pre-to post-task. 3.4 Metacognitive efficiency across conditions

The HMeta-d model converged successfully, with all R ̂ values < 1.1 for both conditions. Posterior estimates, shown in Figure 5A, indicated numerically higher metacognitive efficiency in the calories condition (posterior mean Mratio = 0.88, 95% HDI [0.75, 1.00]) than in the NRF condition (posterior mean Mratio = 0.73, 95% HDI [0.62, 0.84]). However, the posterior distribution of the difference in mu_logMratio (calories -NRF; Figure 5B) had a mean of 0.18 (95% HDI [-0.04, 0.39]), with P(Δ > 0) = 0.95. Although the posterior thus favoured higher efficiency for calorie judgements, the 95% HDI included zero, indicating that the difference was not statistically credible. A Savage-Dickey Bayes factor provided anecdotal evidence against a between-condition difference (BF₀₁ = 2.99).

We performed two additional analyses to further characterise metacognitive efficiency, entering each covariate as a participant-level regressor on log(Mratio) within the hierarchical model. Mean trial-level confidence did not predict Mratio in either condition, with Bayes factors providing strong evidence for the null in the calories condition (BF₀₁ = 14.1) and strong evidence in the NRF condition (BF₀₁ = 10.2). We also examined whether within-participant stimulus variability was related to metacognitive efficiency. Participants whose stimulus differences varied more showed lower Mratio in both conditions (calories: β = -0.19, 95% HDI [-0.34, -0.04]; NRF: β = -0.17, 95% HDI [-0.33, -0.004]), although the Bayes factor provided only weak evidence for an effect in the calories condition (BF₀₁ = 0.48) and was inconclusive in the NRF condition (BF₀₁ = 1.48).

4. Discussion

In this study, we investigated whether objective performance and metacognitive insight can be dissociated across different forms of nutritional judgements and introduced the MetaBites task to test this directly. Participants compared foods on either caloric density or nutritional quality in a 2AFC design with adaptive staircasing, while providing local and global confidence judgements, allowing quantification of metacognitive monitoring at multiple levels. The task demonstrated good construct validity, supporting its use as a measure of nutritional decision-making and confidence. The key result was a dissociation between first-order and second-order performance: judgements of nutritional quality were more accurate and showed higher perceptual sensitivity, whereas calorie judgements elicited higher confidence and more stable task-level global self-evaluation. Metacognitive efficiency, by contrast, did not differ credibly between conditions. Heuristics also predicted judgement behaviour, but at different levels: familiarity predicted choice in opposite directions across conditions, while liking predicted trial-level confidence. Taken together, these findings suggest that nutritional knowledge and the evaluation of that knowledge rely on partially separable processes, shaped by distinct heuristic cues.

Task performance was significantly higher in the NRF as compared to the calories condition across both perceptual sensitivity (d′) and overall accuracy.

However, local confidence was higher in the calories condition, replicating the pattern observed by Lund et al. (2025). This dissociation suggests that metacognitive insight in nutritional judgements is not a straightforward readout of objective ability.

One plausible interpretation is that everyday exposure to calorie information through food packaging and dieting culture may contribute to overall confidence in that domain independently of actual performance (Chua et al., 2012; Metcalfe et al., 1993). Alongside this, calorie judgements can often be made using relatively simple heuristics based on cues such as sugar or fat content (Wang & Begho, 2024), while NRF judgements require integrating multiple nutrients into a less intuitive composite index (Drewnowski, 2009), potentially making performance harder to self-assess (Zhou & Jia, 2023). Regardless of its origins, these differences across nutritional dimensions mirror distinctions consumers encounter in everyday food environments, and may therefore be relevant to understanding dietary decision-making.

The dissociation between performance and metacognitive insight extended to global confidence updating. In the NRF condition, task-level global confidence decreased significantly from pre-to post-task. This pattern of negative updating is incongruent with objective ability, yet consistent with findings from related paradigms (Hoogervorst et al., 2025). Lower local confidence in NRF compared to calories may have contributed to downward adjustment of the global estimate. However, post-task global confidence fell below the mean local confidence, suggesting suboptimal integration into task-level estimates (Rouault et al., 2019), potentially reflecting disproportionate weighting of low-confidence trials. Contrastingly, in the calories condition, task-level global confidence remained stable and reasonably aligned with actual task performance, indicating that subjective monitoring and objective performance were more congruent. One possibility is that greater everyday exposure to calorie information provided a stable prior that anchored global confidence in that condition. The positive association between local and block-level global confidence across both conditions confirms that trial-level confidence was accurately integrated into block-level self-assessments (see Supplementary Figure S4). The updating asymmetry therefore appears specific to task-level summary judgements, not to block-level integration. Whether the stability in the calories condition reflects accurate self-monitoring or a prior belief resistant to updating remains an open question for future work.

Finally, we examined metacognitive efficiency (Mratio) across conditions. The posterior favoured higher efficiency for calorie than nutritional-quality judgements, but the 95% HDI for the difference included zero and a Savage-Dickey Bayes factor gave anecdotal evidence against a between-condition difference. We therefore treat this as, at most, a weak and directionally consistent trend rather than a robust dissociation. At the individual level, mean trial-level confidence did not predict Mratio in either condition, with Bayes factors providing evidence against a relationship between confidence bias and metacognitive efficiency. Participants whose stimulus differences varied more tended to show lower metacognitive efficiency in both conditions, although the evidence for this association was weak. Rahnev and Fleming (2019) reported that adaptive procedures, through the stimulus variability they introduce, can inflate metacognitive estimates. The association observed here runs in the opposite direction. Moreover, all participants underwent the same adaptive procedure, so between-participant variability in stimulus differences reflects individual staircase trajectories rather than a design-level confound, and greater variability may itself index less stable first-order performance. As the association was present in both conditions, it is unlikely to account for the between-condition pattern in Mratio.

Notably, clear condition differences did emerge for first-order accuracy, local confidence, and task-level confidence updating. This indicates that the domains differ in how confident participants felt and how they revised their global selfevaluations, but not detectably in how well trial-level confidence discriminated correct from incorrect responses. One interpretation is that these facets of metacognition are dissociable, with domain sensitivity expressed in confidence bias and global updating rather than in metacognitive efficiency. The efficiency comparison is also the most data-intensive analysis in our design, and the present sample may simply be too small to detect a difference of this size. Although metacognitive efficiency has been shown to vary across cognitive domains, the evidence for domain-specificity is mixed (Baird et al., 2014; Mazancieux et al., 2026; Rouault et al., 2019). Moreover, a difference, or absence of a difference, in Mratio between two tasks does not by itself speak to this question, as a shared metacognitive resource may still yield different efficiencies if one task is noisier than the other. The present design is therefore not suited to address domain-specificity.

Beyond metacognitive measures, this study also revealed that distinct heuristic cues are associated with different levels of nutritional decision-making.

Familiarity predicted first-order choice in both conditions, but in opposite directions: greater familiarity differences increased the probability of selecting the more familiar item in the NRF condition and reduced this probability in the calories condition. The reversal across conditions is best explained by a single underlying heuristic: familiar foods are perceived as more nutritious and lower in calories. This is consistent with prior work showing that familiarity is associated with altered nutritional perception (Benson et al., 2018; Pinto et al., 2021). Furthermore, item-level choice proportions across the two conditions were strongly negatively correlated, confirming that participants treated calories and nutritional quality as opposing dimensions of the same "healthiness" judgement, in line with the categorical framing described by Manippa et al. (2020) and Rozin et al. (1996). A different pattern emerged for confidence: familiarity did not track trial-level confidence, whereas larger liking differences predicted higher confidence in both conditions, independent of trial difficulty. This result did not replicate the pattern predicted by cue-familiarity accounts of confidence (Metcalfe et al., 1993) and suggests that affective rather than familiarity-based cues may contribute to metacognitive monitoring in nutritional judgements. This is consistent with accounts in which affective reactions to stimuli, including how pleasant or aversive they are perceived to be, function as an independent input to metacognitive judgement alongside cognitive cues (Efklides, 2006).

Several limitations of the present study warrant consideration. First, although the staircasing procedure showed adequate convergence overall, the calories condition had not fully converged by the end of the task. This likely reflects strong prior beliefs about caloric content interfering with the adaptive adjustment process.

However, the absolute deviation from the target was small (1.1 percentage points) and stable across burn-in thresholds (Supplementary S2, Table S1), suggesting this is unlikely to introduce considerable implications for the validity of the findings.

Nonetheless, this could reflect that adaptive staircasing is generally better suited to perceptual discrimination than semantic knowledge paradigms (Morales et al., 2018; Rahnev & Fleming, 2019). Moreover, performance differences between conditions may partly reflect the narrower NRF stimulus distribution, which can increase the likelihood of unintended difficulty deviations. Expanding the NRF stimulus set would improve staircase convergence in future iterations of the task. Caloric density is a familiar, unidimensional metric that can be approximated using simple heuristics (e.g., fat or sugar content), whereas the NRF index is less familiar and integrates twelve nutrients across two categories. Representational complexity and prior exposure therefore covary with the intended domain manipulation, and betweencondition differences cannot be attributed to the domain manipulation alone. Notably, participants' choice responses were more accurate in the NRF condition, with comparable response times. Reduced knowledge access to NRF would predict slower and less accurate responses rather than the observed pattern. This is further supported by the strong negative item-level correlation between calorie and NRF choice proportions, as participants appear to have interpreted both conditions as opposite ends of the same "healthiness" judgement. Isolating the contribution of these factors will require future designs that vary them independently. No a priori power analysis was conducted, and the present study should be considered exploratory given the modest sample size of healthy young adults. Replication in larger, more diverse samples will be needed to characterise individual differences and enable comparisons between clinical and non-clinical populations. Lastly, establishing test-retest reliability and convergent validity against established metacognitive paradigms (e.g., perceptual or semantic-memory tasks) will further support the task's use as a research tool.

In conclusion, the MetaBites task demonstrated adequate validity as a measure of nutritional decision-making and metacognitive monitoring. The task revealed a dissociation between objective performance and metacognitive insight in nutritional judgements, suggesting that nutritional knowledge and its evaluation rely on partially separable mechanisms. Critically, the type of nutritional information, caloric density or nutritional quality, selectively modulated metacognitive access in the opposite direction to first-order performance. Confidence was higher in the condition with lower accuracy, suggesting that individuals may overestimate their judgements in the domain where they are most prone to error. This miscalibration suggests that nutritional literacy and its metacognitive evaluation may be dissociable, with the latter potentially representing an underexplored component of nutritional decision-making (Cohen & Zion, 2020). Whether such dissociations are present or more pronounced in clinical populations remains to be established. The MetaBites task offers a promising tool for investigating this, particularly in individuals with disturbed eating behaviours where metacognitive deficits have previously been reported (Aloi et al., 2024; Olstad et al., 2015). Beyond characterising such deficits, identifying where miscalibration occurs could help identify individuals at elevated cognitive risk before the onset of disordered eating and provide a specific target for early intervention (Colton et al., 2024). The paradigm can also be extended to examine how nutritional metacognition connects to related processes such as interoceptive monitoring and body image. The finding that metacognitive insight and objective performance can systematically diverge in nutritional judgements points to an underexplored pathway through which knowledge fails to translate into behaviour.

These findings identify nutrition as a domain where metacognitive miscalibration operates in condition-specific ways, extending the argument that metacognition is especially consequential in complex, contested information environments (Fischer & Fleming, 2024). Closing this gap may require addressing not only what people know about nutrition, but how accurately they know it.

S3: Repeated stimulus pairs and task performance

To address whether repeated exposures to the same stimulus pair affected behaviour, we identified all pairs presented more than once within a condition (Calories: 7.9% of pairs; NRF: 4.7%) and examined choice consistency and confidence across repetitions. Participants chose the same item as on the first exposure on most repeated trials (second exposure: Calories 87.2%, NRF 91.6%; third exposure: Calories 80.0%, NRF 54.5%, based on 20 and 11 trials). This exceeds the consistency expected if each choice were made independently at the observed accuracy (Calories 60.5%, NRF 66.1%), consistent with stable item-level beliefs and possibly memory for earlier responses. A GLMM predicting repetition of the first-exposure choice showed no effect of repetition number (β = -0.50, z = -0.80, p = .425) and no significant repetition × Condition interaction (β = -1.80, z = -1.90, p = .058). Individual consistency ranged from 0.25 to 1.00 (SD = 0.18) in the calories condition and from 0.50 to 1.00 (SD = 0.13) in the NRF condition; adding a random slope for repetition did not improve fit (χ²(2) = 0.07, p = .966). Trial-level confidence showed no effect of repetition (β = 0.043, SE = 0.053, p = .412) or interaction with Condition (β = -0.023, p = .786). Given that repeated pairs made up a small proportion of trials, reuse of earlier responses is unlikely to have materially affected the main results. cluster-bootstrap resamples of participants. All correlations between local and block-level global confidence were significant (all Holm-corrected p = .003, the smallest value attainable with 2,000 resamples). Mean local confidence across all trials was the strongest predictor of block-level global confidence (β = .54, p < .001), with a small additional recency effect from the last 5 trials (β = .13, p = .019) and no primacy effect from the first 5 trials (β = .07, p = .225). Within the calories condition, the correlation with the full block was stronger than with either the first 5 (Holm-corrected p = .030) or last 5 trials (p = .021); in the NRF condition this pattern did not survive correction (both p = .13). No significant between-condition differences were observed in any window (all Holm-corrected p = 1.00).
